title: Methotrexate: Weekly Dosing and Multisystem Toxicity
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: For many non-cancer indications, oral methotrexate is taken once weekly—not daily. Accidental daily dosing has caused fatal toxicity. Monitor marrow, liver, lungs, kidneys, GI mucosa, pregnancy risk, and interacting medications.
recognize: Mouth sores, fever/infection, unusual bruising, severe diarrhea, jaundice, new cough or dyspnea, and renal decline can signal serious toxicity.
The current U.S. label carries a boxed warning for medication-error deaths from inadvertent daily dosing.
priorities: Verify indication and exact dosing schedule before administration.
Stop and escalate suspected daily-vs-weekly medication error immediately.
Review CBC, renal/liver monitoring and pregnancy precautions as ordered.
assessMonitor: CBC, liver tests, renal function, pulmonary symptoms, oral/GI mucosa, infection signs, pregnancy risk, and medication interactions.
interventions: Administer folate supplementation when prescribed for inflammatory-disease regimens.
Use infection precautions appropriate to degree of immunosuppression.
medicationSafety: Pregnancy is contraindicated for non-neoplastic indications.
NSAIDs and other interacting drugs can increase toxicity in selected circumstances.
Daily administration in place of weekly dosing is a high-risk medication error.
teaching: For weekly regimens, use a specific day of the week and confirm the label every time.
Report mouth sores, fever, bleeding, jaundice, or new breathing symptoms promptly.
delegationScope: Medication schedule verification and toxicity assessment require licensed-nurse judgment; high-risk administration follows facility policy.
examTrap: Reading 'once weekly' as 'once daily' because most oral medications are daily.
oneLinePearl: Methotrexate: weekly means weekly—daily can kill.
sourceBasis: DailyMed Methotrexate Tablets Prescribing Information, boxed warning revised 2026

title: Hydroxychloroquine: Retina and Cardiac Safety
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Hydroxychloroquine requires attention to retinal toxicity, cardiomyopathy/conduction disease, QT prolongation, hypoglycemia, and dose accumulation in susceptible patients. New visual change, syncope, palpitations, or unexplained hypoglycemia needs prompt evaluation.
recognize: Blurred vision, field defects, difficulty reading, or color changes can indicate retinal toxicity.
QT prolongation and cardiomyopathy are uncommon but potentially life-threatening.
priorities: Verify baseline/periodic ophthalmic monitoring according to risk and duration.
Review QT-prolonging drugs and cardiac history.
Escalate visual or rhythm symptoms promptly.
assessMonitor: Vision symptoms/exams, ECG when clinically indicated, glucose symptoms, renal/hepatic function when relevant, and treatment response.
interventions: Coordinate ophthalmology follow-up rather than relying on bedside acuity alone.
medicationSafety: Concomitant QT-prolonging drugs can increase arrhythmia risk.
Retinal injury can progress even after the drug is stopped.
teaching: Keep eye-monitoring appointments and report any new vision change promptly.
Review all new medications for interaction risk.
delegationScope: Routine administration may follow local scope; vision or cardiac toxicity assessment requires licensed/provider escalation.
examTrap: Assuming a rheumatology drug only needs symptom monitoring and forgetting eye and cardiac surveillance.
oneLinePearl: Hydroxychloroquine: protect the retina and respect the QT.

title: Allopurinol: Rash Means Stop and Escalate
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Allopurinol lowers uric-acid production for gout prevention; it does not rapidly relieve an acute gout flare. Any new rash can signal severe hypersensitivity and requires immediate discontinuation/escalation according to the current label.
recognize: SJS/TEN/DRESS and systemic hypersensitivity can occur, especially early in therapy.
HLA-B*58:01 increases severe hypersensitivity risk and targeted screening may be considered for higher-prevalence populations before treatment.
priorities: Ask about rash, fever, facial swelling, mucosal lesions, liver symptoms, and renal status.
Stop and escalate any new rash or hypersensitivity finding per protocol.
Reinforce that flare-prevention therapy may continue long term when tolerated.
assessMonitor: Skin/mucosa, renal function, liver tests when indicated, uric acid, gout-flare frequency, and interacting drugs.
interventions: Promote hydration when appropriate and reinforce adherence to prophylactic therapy.
medicationSafety: Renal impairment may require dose adjustment.
Certain antibiotics and thiazides can increase rash/hypersensitivity risk in susceptible patients.
teaching: Stop the drug and seek prompt medical advice for any rash.
Do not expect allopurinol to act like an immediate pain reliever during an acute flare.
delegationScope: Rash and systemic hypersensitivity findings require licensed-nurse assessment and provider escalation.
examTrap: Giving another dose despite a new rash because it looks mild.
oneLinePearl: Allopurinol rash is never a 'watch and wait' finding.

title: Colchicine: GI Toxicity and Interaction Danger
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Colchicine reduces inflammation in gout and selected inflammatory conditions but has a narrow safety margin. Severe diarrhea/vomiting, muscle weakness, cytopenias, or toxicity after CYP3A4/P-gp interactions—especially with renal/hepatic impairment—requires urgent review.
recognize: GI toxicity often precedes more severe toxicity.
Neuromuscular toxicity and rhabdomyolysis risk rise with renal dysfunction and interacting drugs such as some macrolides or statins.
priorities: Review renal/hepatic function and interacting medications.
Report severe or persistent GI symptoms rather than automatically treating through them.
Escalate new muscle weakness or dark urine.
assessMonitor: GI symptoms, CBC when indicated, CK/muscle symptoms, renal/hepatic function, and interaction profile.
interventions: Avoid adding potent CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitors without clinician review.
medicationSafety: Certain strong CYP3A4 or P-gp inhibitors can make colchicine dangerously toxic.
Dose and frequency depend on indication and organ function.
teaching: Do not exceed the prescribed regimen and check before starting new antibiotics or other interacting drugs.
delegationScope: Toxicity assessment and interaction decisions require licensed/provider review.
examTrap: Assuming severe diarrhea is just an expected nuisance rather than an early toxicity warning.
oneLinePearl: Colchicine toxicity often starts in the gut before it reaches the muscles and marrow.

title: Epoetin Alfa: Hemoglobin Target and Thrombosis Risk
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Epoetin alfa stimulates red-cell production but can increase hypertension and thromboembolic/cardiovascular risk if hemoglobin rises too high or too quickly. Iron availability is necessary for an adequate response.
recognize: Poor response may reflect iron deficiency, inflammation, bleeding, infection, or inadequate dialysis/other causes.
Headache, hypertension, chest pain, neurologic symptoms, or limb swelling can signal complications.
priorities: Verify hemoglobin trend and ordered hold/adjustment parameters.
Assess BP and iron status as ordered.
Escalate chest pain, focal neurologic deficit, or VTE symptoms.
assessMonitor: Hemoglobin/hematocrit, BP, iron studies, dialysis adequacy when relevant, thrombosis symptoms, and treatment response.
interventions: Administer iron replacement when prescribed and indicated.
Avoid chasing a normal hemoglobin target when the therapeutic plan specifies a lower safe target.
medicationSafety: Higher hemoglobin targets can increase cardiovascular/thrombotic harm.
Rapid rises require dose review according to the prescribing plan.
teaching: Keep lab appointments and report clot or stroke symptoms immediately.
delegationScope: Routine administration may follow local scope; dose-hold interpretation and adverse-event assessment require licensed/provider review.
examTrap: Trying to normalize hemoglobin completely instead of following the ordered risk-balanced target.
oneLinePearl: ESA therapy is about enough red cells—not the highest hemoglobin possible.

title: Filgrastim: Neutrophil Recovery and Rare Emergencies
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Filgrastim stimulates neutrophil production and commonly causes bone pain. Rare but serious complications include splenic rupture, acute respiratory distress, severe allergic reactions, and capillary-leak syndromes.
recognize: Bone pain is common as marrow activity increases.
Left upper abdominal or shoulder pain can signal splenic enlargement/rupture.
New dyspnea/hypoxemia requires evaluation rather than assuming infection alone.
priorities: Trend ANC/CBC according to the oncology plan.
Escalate LUQ/shoulder pain, respiratory distress, or anaphylaxis immediately.
Use prescribed pain management for expected bone pain.
assessMonitor: CBC/ANC, bone pain, spleen symptoms, respiratory status, allergic reaction, and treatment timing relative to chemotherapy.
interventions: Administer according to oncology timing instructions and product-specific handling.
medicationSafety: Timing around cytotoxic chemotherapy matters and follows protocol.
Different G-CSF products are not automatically interchangeable without the treatment plan.
teaching: Bone pain can occur, but severe left-sided abdominal/shoulder pain or breathing difficulty is urgent.
delegationScope: Administration follows oncology/state policy; assessment of acute complications requires licensed-nurse escalation.
examTrap: Calling all pain after filgrastim expected bone pain and missing splenic rupture.
oneLinePearl: Filgrastim grows neutrophils; LUQ pain is not routine bone pain.

title: Oral Iron: Absorption, Stool, and Adherence
bottomLine: Oral iron treats iron deficiency, not every anemia. Dark stool and GI upset are common; constipation and poor adherence are frequent barriers. Improvement in hemoglobin does not remove the need to identify the cause of iron deficiency.
recognize: Dark stools are expected but tarry stool with instability can still represent GI bleeding.
Iron absorption can be reduced by antacids, calcium, and some foods/drugs depending on timing.
priorities: Confirm iron deficiency and the prescribed elemental-iron regimen.
Assess constipation, nausea, adherence, and ongoing blood loss.
Keep liquid iron away from teeth or use administration techniques that reduce staining.
assessMonitor: Hemoglobin, ferritin/iron indices when ordered, GI tolerance, stool pattern, adherence, and source-of-loss evaluation.
interventions: Use dietary iron education as an adjunct rather than a substitute for replacement when deficiency is significant.
medicationSafety: Iron overdose is especially dangerous in children; store securely.
Separate from interacting medications when instructed.
teaching: Expect darker stool, follow timing instructions, and keep iron locked away from children.
delegationScope: Routine administration may be delegated only as permitted; evaluation of ongoing bleeding or treatment failure requires licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Assuming black stool on iron can never be GI bleeding.
oneLinePearl: Iron darkens stool—but clinical bleeding still needs assessment.
sourceBasis: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements Iron Guidance

title: Mycophenolate: Infection, Marrow, and Pregnancy Risk
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Mycophenolate suppresses lymphocyte proliferation to prevent rejection but increases serious-infection and malignancy risk, can suppress blood counts, and is highly teratogenic. Pregnancy-prevention requirements and laboratory monitoring are central to safe use.
recognize: Fever, sore throat, unusual bruising, or persistent diarrhea can reflect infection, cytopenia, or drug toxicity.
Pregnancy exposure carries major fetal risk.
priorities: Monitor CBC and infection symptoms.
Verify reproductive-safety counselling and contraception plan when applicable.
Escalate severe diarrhea, infection, or cytopenic symptoms.
assessMonitor: CBC, renal/hepatic function when indicated, GI tolerance, infection signs, pregnancy risk, and transplant rejection symptoms.
interventions: Use sun protection and skin-surveillance teaching because malignancy risk rises with immunosuppression.
medicationSafety: Do not interchange formulations casually because exposure may differ.
Antacids and other products can alter absorption depending on formulation/timing.
teaching: Use required pregnancy prevention, report infection promptly, and do not stop transplant immunosuppression independently.
delegationScope: Immunosuppressant monitoring and pregnancy-risk counselling require licensed/provider oversight.
examTrap: Stopping mycophenolate during a mild illness without contacting the transplant team.
oneLinePearl: Mycophenolate protects the graft by suppressing immunity—watch infection, marrow, and pregnancy risk.

title: Tacrolimus: Levels, Kidneys, Potassium, Infection
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Tacrolimus is a calcineurin-inhibitor immunosuppressant with a boxed warning for serious infections and malignancies. It also causes nephrotoxicity, neurotoxicity, hyperkalemia, hypertension, and major CYP3A interactions; therapeutic drug monitoring matters.
recognize: Rising creatinine, reduced urine output, tremor, headache, confusion, seizures, hyperkalemia, or hypertension can indicate toxicity.
Grapefruit and potent CYP3A inhibitors can raise tacrolimus levels.
priorities: Verify trough/level timing according to transplant protocol.
Trend renal function, potassium, BP, glucose, and neurologic findings.
Escalate severe neurotoxicity, renal decline, infection, or rejection symptoms.
assessMonitor: Tacrolimus concentrations, creatinine/eGFR, potassium, magnesium, BP, glucose, neurologic status, infection, and interacting medications.
interventions: Maintain consistent administration relative to food according to the prescribed product plan.
Use sun protection and infection-prevention education.
medicationSafety: Immediate- and extended-release tacrolimus products are not automatically interchangeable.
Grapefruit/CYP3A inhibitors can markedly increase exposure.
Nephrotoxic combinations require caution.
teaching: Take the same formulation exactly as directed, avoid grapefruit, and check before starting new prescriptions or supplements.
delegationScope: Therapeutic-level interpretation and transplant medication changes require specialist/licensed-provider oversight.
examTrap: Treating all tacrolimus formulations as interchangeable or ignoring a new interacting medication.
oneLinePearl: Tacrolimus: level, kidneys, potassium, nerves, interactions.
sourceBasis: DailyMed Tacrolimus Capsules Prescribing Information, revised 2026

title: Dantrolene: Malignant Hyperthermia Rescue Drug
bottomLine: Dantrolene is the specific treatment for malignant hyperthermia. When unexplained rapid rise in end-tidal CO2, muscle rigidity, tachycardia, acidosis, hyperkalemia, and later hyperthermia occur after triggering anesthetic exposure, activate the malignant-hyperthermia protocol and give dantrolene promptly.
recognize: Hyperthermia can be a late sign; rising CO2 and rigidity may appear earlier.
Succinylcholine and volatile anesthetics are classic triggers in susceptible patients.
priorities: Stop triggering agents and activate the MH response.
Hyperventilate with 100% oxygen and administer dantrolene according to emergency protocol.
Treat hyperkalemia, acidosis, arrhythmia, and hyperthermia while monitoring urine output.
assessMonitor: End-tidal CO2, temperature, rhythm, potassium, blood gases, CK, urine color/output, coagulation, and recurrence after initial stabilization.
interventions: Use active cooling when indicated and stop cooling before overshoot hypothermia.
Prepare for prolonged monitoring because recrudescence can occur.
medicationSafety: Dantrolene reconstitution and dosing are protocol-driven emergency tasks.
Calcium-channel blocker combinations with dantrolene are avoided in MH management because of hyperkalemia/cardiovascular-collapse risk.
teaching: After recovery, patients need documentation of MH susceptibility and referral for family/genetic counselling/testing as appropriate.
delegationScope: MH is a perioperative emergency; LPN/LVN roles depend on setting competency, but recognition, immediate emergency activation, and assigned protocol tasks are urgent.
examTrap: Waiting for a very high temperature before suspecting malignant hyperthermia.
oneLinePearl: MH: rising CO2 and rigidity come before the dramatic fever—give dantrolene fast.
